Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verses 3–4:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾, that is, the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), or the night of the middle of Sha'ban. It was also said that between it and the Night of Power there are forty nights. The majority hold the first view, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], and His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. The Night of Power, according to most of the opinions, is in the month of Ramadan. Then they said: He sent it down all at once from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya), then Jibril brought it down to His Prophet (ﷺ) at the time when the need arose. It was also said: the beginning of its descent was in the Night of Power. And "al-mubarakah" (the blessed): the one abundant in good, because of the good and blessing that descend in it, and because supplications are answered in it. Even if nothing else were found in it except the sending down of the Qur'an alone, that would suffice as a blessing.

﴿Indeed, We are ever warners﴾, ﴿in it every matter is made distinct﴾. These are two resumptive, enveloping sentences (jumlatan mustanafatan, malfufatan), by which the answer to the oath is explained, as if it were said: We sent it down because it is among Our affairs to warn and to caution against punishment, and Our sending it down in this particular night was specifically because the sending down of the Qur'an is among wise matters, and this night is the place where every wise matter is made distinct. The meaning of "yufraq" (is made distinct): it is detailed and recorded, every matter, of the provisions of the servants, their terms of life, and all their affairs, from this night until the Night of Power that comes in the coming year.

﴿Wise﴾: possessing wisdom, i.e., decreed in accordance with what wisdom requires. This is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), because wisdom is in truth an attribute of the one who issues the command, and he attributed it to the matter metaphorically.

﴿A command from Us﴾ is in the accusative as an object of specification (*ikhtisas*, a grammatical construction that singles out a noun for emphasis). He made every command grand and majestic by describing it as ﴿wise﴾. Then he increased its grandeur and majesty by saying: "By this command I mean a command issuing from Us, as Our knowledge and Our governance require."

﴿Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ is a *badal* (substitution or apposition, in which a following phrase restates a preceding one) for "Indeed, We were ever warning [messengers]."

Mercy from your Lord. It is a object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: "We sent down the Qur'an because it is among Our way and custom to send Messengers with Books to Our servants for the sake of mercy upon them." Or it is an explanation (ta'lil) of His words "a command from Us." And "mercy" may be an object (maf'ul bihi), and He has described mercy with sending, just as He described it with it in His words: ﴿Whatever He grants to mankind of mercy, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him﴾ [Fatir: 2]. The original form would be: "Indeed We were sending (Messengers) as a mercy from Us," but the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that lordship (rububiyyah) necessitates mercy upon those who are nurtured.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing﴾, of their words,

﴿the All-Knowing﴾, of their conditions.

﴿Rabb﴾ (Lord): the Kufan [grammarians] read it in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "Rabbika," while others read it in the nominative, meaning "He is the Lord."

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain.﴾ The sense of the condition is that they used to acknowledge that the heavens and the earth have a Lord and Creator. It was said to them: indeed, the sending of the messengers and the sending down of the Books is a mercy from the Lord. Then it was said: this Lord is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, whom you acknowledge and admit is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if your acknowledgment is from knowledge and certainty, just as you say: "This is the generosity of Zayd, whose generosity people have heard of, if its report has reached you and you have been told its story."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 8:

﴿There is no god but He; He gives life and causes death; your Lord﴾, i.e., He is your Lord,

﴿and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the preceding (ʿaṭf: grammatical coordination, joining a word to a preceding one), and then He returned [the matter] to their being certain (yūqinīn), by His saying:
﴿Nay, but they are in doubt, playing.﴾ And their affirmation does not proceed from knowledge and certainty; rather, it is a statement mixed with mockery and play.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 10:

﴿So watch for them﴾, wait for them,

﴿on the day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke﴾, a smoke that comes from the sky before the Day of Resurrection, entering into the ears of the disbelievers, until the head of each one becomes like a roasted head (al-ra's al-hanidh), and the believer is afflicted by it in the manner of a cold (al-zukam), and the whole earth becomes like a house that has been set alight within, with no gaps in it. It has also been said that when the Quraysh persisted in their opposition to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, press down Your hand upon Mudar, and make it for them years like the years of Yusuf." So famine struck them until they ate carrion and al-'ilhiz (a blood-and-hair mixture, a kind of food made from blood and hair of camels, pressed and eaten in famine). A man would see smoke between the sky and the earth, and when he spoke to a man, he would hear his speech but not see him, because of the smoke.

﴿visible﴾, its state is manifest, and no one doubts that it is smoke.

﴿Yaghshā al-nās﴾ (it covers the people), meaning it envelops them and clothes them with itself; it is in the genitive position as an attributive adjective (ṣifah) [of "smoke" in the preceding verse],

﴿Hādhā ʿadhābun alīm﴾ (This is a painful punishment).

That is: "We will believe if You remove the punishment from us." It is in the accusative position (manṣūb al-maḥall), governed by an implied verb, which is "يَقُولُونَ" (yaqūlūna, "they say"). And "يَقُولُونَ" is itself in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: saying that.

(p-289) "How can they have the reminder?" How could they be mindful, take heed, and keep the promise they made of faith when the punishment is lifted?

"And a clear messenger had come to them. Then they turned away from him and said, 'A taught one, a madman!'" Meaning: there had already come to them what is greater and more compelling for remembrance than the lifting of the smoke, namely what appeared upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of signs and clear proofs, including the inimitable Book and other things. Yet they did not take heed, they turned away from him, and they slandered him, claiming that 'Addas, a foreign slave belonging to some of the Thaqif, was the one who taught him, and they attributed him to madness.

Translation:

﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little,﴾ a little time, or a little removal,

﴿indeed, you will return﴾ to the disbelief in which you were, or to the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 16:

﴿On the Day We will seize with the greatest seizure﴾: it is the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of Badr.

﴿Indeed, We will take retribution﴾: that is, We will take retribution against them on that day. The accusative of "yawma nabtishu" (on the day We seize) is governed by "udhkurū" (remember), with what is indicated by "innā muntaqimūn" (indeed We take retribution), which is "nantaqimu" (We take retribution), and not by "muntaqimūn" itself, because what comes after "inna" (indeed) does not govern what comes before it.

﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh﴾: before these polytheists, meaning We dealt with them in the manner of one who tests, so that what was hidden within them would become manifest.

﴿and there came to them a noble Messenger﴾: noble before Allah and before His believing servants. Or he was noble in himself, of lofty lineage and good descent, because Allah (Exalted is He) never sent a prophet except from among the chiefs and noblest of his people.

﴿That deliver to me﴾: here "an" is the **an mufassira** (the explanatory "an"), because the coming of a messenger to those he is sent to implies the meaning of speech, since he comes to them only as a bringer of good news, a warner, and one who calls to God. Alternatively, it is the **mukhaffafa** (the lightened form) of the **thaqila** (heavy form, i.e., "anna"), and its meaning is: "And he came to them saying that the matter and the word are: Deliver to me, submit to me."

﴿servants of God﴾: this is the object (**maf'ul bihi**) of the verb. They are the Children of Israel. The meaning is: "Deliver them to me and send them with me," like His saying: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. It is also permissible that it be a vocative address to them, in the sense of: "Deliver to me, servants of God, what is obligatory for you toward me (p-٢٩٠), of belief in me, acceptance of my call, and following my way." He gave the reason for this in His saying: ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾, i.e., concerning my message, not one accused.

"And do not exalt yourselves against Allah." The "an" here is like the first one in both its possible readings: meaning "do not be arrogant toward Allah by treating His Messenger and His revelation with contempt," or "do not be arrogant toward the Prophet of Allah."

﴿Indeed, I am bringing you a clear authority﴾: a manifest proof that shows I am a Prophet.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 20:

﴿And indeed I have sought refuge﴾, idghām (assimilation of the two identical letters) by Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and 'Ali,

﴿in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾, that is, lest you kill me by stoning. Its meaning is that he takes refuge in his Lord, relying on the fact that He will protect him from them and from their plotting, so he is unconcerned with what they threatened him with of stoning and killing.

The Qur'an verse is "And if you do not believe in me, then leave me alone (fa'tazilun)" (44:21).

Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) of al-Nasafi: That is, if you do not believe in me, then there is no friendship (muwalah) between me and those who do not believe. So withdraw from me, or leave me alone in a state of neutrality, neither for me nor against me, and do not harm me with your evil and your injury. For the recompense of one who calls you to that in which your success lies is not that: "tarjumuni" (you would stone me), "fa'tazilun" (leave me alone), in both cases. "Ya'qub" (a reading attributed to Ya'qub al-Hadrami).

﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾, complaining about his people,

﴿that these are a people who are criminals﴾. That is, *bi-anna hā'ulā'*, meaning he called upon his Lord with this. It was said: his supplication was, "O Allah, hasten for them what they deserve for their crimes." It was also said: it is his saying, ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the people who are wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 85]. It is read as *innа hā'ulā'* with a kasra on the *inna*, on the basis of *idmar al-qawl* (an ellipsis of the verb "to say"). That is: "So he called upon his Lord and said: 'Indeed, these...'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 23:

﴿Fa-asri﴾, from "asra" (to travel by night), "fa-isri" with a wasl (connected) reading, is the reading of the Hijazi (Meccan and Medinan) reciters, from "sara" (to travel by night). The verb of saying is implied after the fa', meaning: "So he said: Travel [by night]",

﴿with My servants﴾, that is, the Children of Israel,

﴿by night, for you will be pursued﴾, that is: "God arranged that you should go ahead, and Pharaoh and his hosts would follow you, so that He would save those who went ahead and drown those who followed."

(p-291) ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, still, calm. Moses (peace be upon him), when he had crossed the sea, wanted to strike it with his staff so that it would close back over them. He was commanded to leave it still in its state, remaining as it was, with the water standing upright and the path dry, not striking it with his staff and not changing anything of it, so that the Copts would enter it; and when they were inside it, God would close it over them. It has also been said that "al-rahw" means a wide opening, i.e., leave it open as it is, spread apart.

﴿Indeed, they are an army that will be drowned﴾, after your coming out of the sea. It is also read with a fatḥah (i.e., "because they"), meaning "for they".

"How many" (kam), an expression for abundance, is in the accusative, governed by His saying: ﴿They left behind gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾. The "noble station" is what they had of fine dwellings; it is said that it means pulpits.

[Quran 44:27] "And luxury" — ease and comfort (taannum),

"in which they had been jesting" — enjoying themselves (mutanaʿimin).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 28:

﴿Kadhalika﴾ (So it is): meaning, the matter is thus. The kaf (ك) here is in the place of nominative case, as the predicate of an implied subject (mubtada' muḍmar), i.e., the matter is "like that."

﴿And We bequeathed them to another people﴾, who had no connection with them whatsoever, neither by kinship, nor by religion, nor by allegiance; and they were the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 29:

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾, because they died as disbelievers. When a believer dies, the heaven and the earth weep over him: the earth weeps over the believer through his place of prayer (muṣallā), and the heaven through the ascent point of his deeds (maṣ‘ad ‘amalihi). And it is related from al-Ḥasan: "the people of the heaven and the earth."

﴿And they were not given respite﴾, i.e., they were not deferred to another time, and they were not granted a delay.

Surah 44, verse 30:

﴿And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment﴾ — i.e., enslavement, subjugation, and the killing of their sons.

"From Pharaoh" — a substitute (badal) for "the humiliating torment," with the preposition repeated, as if he himself were a humiliating torment, owing to his excessiveness in tormenting them and humiliating them. Or it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "that is from Pharaoh."

﴿Indeed he was haughty﴾, arrogant.

﴿among the transgressors﴾: a second predicate, i.e., "he was arrogant and a transgressor."

(p-292) ﴿And We chose them﴾, that is, the Children of Israel,

﴿knowingly over the worlds﴾. "Knowingly" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring to the subject pronoun (of the verb "chose"): that is, [We chose them] while knowing the place of election and that they were deserving of being chosen,

﴿over the worlds﴾, over the worlds of their time.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 33:

﴿And We gave them of the signs that which contained a manifest trial,﴾ such as the splitting of the sea, the shading of the clouds, the sending down of the manna and the quail, and other than that.

﴿A manifest trial﴾ means a clear blessing, or a clear test, so that We may see how you act.

﴿Indeed these﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh,

﴿are surely saying﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 35:

﴿In hiya﴾, meaning: what is "al-mawta" (the death)

﴿illa mawtatuna al-ula﴾ ("It is only our first death"). The difficulty is that the discourse concerns the second life, not death, so why was it not said: "In hiya illa hayatuna al-ula" ("It is only our first life")? And what is the meaning of mentioning "the first," as if they had been promised a second death, so that they denied it and affirmed the first? The answer is that it was said to them: "You will die a death that is followed by a life, just as a death preceded you that was followed by a life." This is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. They said: "It is only our first death," meaning: the death that is of such a nature as to be followed by a life is none other than the first death. Thus there is no difference, in meaning, between this and His saying: "except our worldly life." It is also possible that this is a denial of what is in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and given us life twice﴾ [Ghafir: 11]. ﴿And we are not to be raised﴾, meaning: not to be resurrected. It is said: "Anshara Allah al-mawta" and "nasharahum," when He resurrects them (the dead).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 36:

﴿Then bring back our fathers﴾, an address to those who were promising them resurrection, namely the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers.

﴿If you are truthful﴾, i.e., if you speak the truth in what you say, then hasten for us the bringing back to life of those of our fathers who have died, by your asking your Lord for that, so that it may be a proof that what you promise of the establishment of the Hour and the resurrection of the dead is true.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 37:

﴿Are they better⁠—﴾, in strength and power,

﴿or the people of Tubba'⁠﴾, that is, Tubba' al-Himyari (the title of the kings of Yemen), who was a believer, while his people were disbelievers. It is also said that he was a prophet. And in a hadith: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not."

﴿and those before them⁠﴾, in the nominative case by coordination with "the people of Tubba'".

﴿We destroyed them; indeed they were criminals⁠﴾, disbelievers, deniers of the Resurrection.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ — i.e., what is between the two kinds (jinn and mankind),

﴿playing﴾ — a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Had there been no resurrection, no reckoning, and no reward, the creation of creatures would have been solely for annihilation, and so it would be play.

We did not create them except with truth (ﷺ)... wait, no honorific appears here, so I render the passage as it stands.

**Translation:**

﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾, meaning with earnestness, the opposite of play.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾, that it was created for this purpose.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the Day of Decision﴾, between the one who is in the right and the one who is in falsehood, and it is the Day of Resurrection,

﴿Its appointed time for them all﴾, the time of their appointment, all of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 44, verse 41:

﴿On the Day when no close friend (*mawla*, patron or protector) will avail any close friend anything﴾. That is: *walī* (close friend), whatever kind of close friend, against whatever kind of close friend, [will avail] anything of averting [harm], that is, even a little of it.

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾. The pronoun refers to *mawla*, and it is plural in meaning because the word, being indefinite and general, encompasses every *mawla*.

Qur'anic quotations: "except those on whom Allah has mercy" is in the nominative position, as a substitute (badal) for the waw in "yunsarun" (they are helped). That is: none is kept back from the punishment except those whom Allah has shown mercy to.

"Indeed He is the Mighty" — the Overpowering over His enemies,

"the Merciful" — toward His friends.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 43:

﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum﴾: it is in the likeness of the trees of this world, but it is in the Fire. Its fruit is the zaqqum, and it is every food that is heavy (thaqil).

(p-294) ﴿طَعامُ الأثِيمِ﴾ ("the food of the sinner" — Qur'an 44:44): he is the wicked one, the one who commits many sins. It is reported from Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was teaching a man to recite, and the man would say "طَعامُ اليَتِيمِ" (ṭaʿām al-yatīm, "the food of the orphan"), whereupon he said: "Say: ṭaʿām al-fājir (the food of the wicked one), O man." From this you may infer that substituting one word for another is permissible provided the word conveys its meaning. On this basis Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) permitted reciting the Qur'an in Persian, on condition that the reciter conveys all of its meanings in their entirety, without omitting any of them. They said: this condition indicates that it is a permission in the sense of "no permission," because in the speech of the Arabs — especially in the Qur'an, which is miraculous in its eloquence, the strangeness of its composition and its styles — there are subtle meanings and fine distinctions that no tongue, whether Persian or other, can independently convey. It is related that he returned to their view (i.e., of the two companions), and it is upon this that reliance is placed.

["Like murky oil-dregs"] — "al-muhl" is the dregs of oil, and the kaf (ك) is in the nominative case, being a predicate following another predicate.

"It boils in the bellies" — with the ya' (ي), read by Makki and Hafs, so the verb is in the masculine form; with the ta' (ت), the reading refers to the tree (al-shajara), and with the ya', to the food (al-ta'am).

﴿كَالْمُهْلِ﴾ — "Like the molten metal (al-muhl)" is the standard rendering; the passage as given glosses al-muhl as dregs of oil (durdi al-zayt), so the translation follows the commentary's gloss.

Correction to the translation above: I must render the text as it stands, so here is the faithful version:

﴿Seize him﴾, i.e., the sinner;

﴿then drag him﴾, drag him with violence and harshness. "fa'tulūhu" (with damma on the ʿayn-less alif-form), "Makki, Nafi', Shami, Sahl and Ya'qub" [read it this way];

﴿into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, into its middle and its greater part.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 48:

﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of the boiling water.﴾ The thing poured is the boiling water (al-hamim), not its torment; however, when the boiling water is poured over him, its torment and its severity have indeed been poured over him. The pouring of torment is a metaphor (isti'arah), and it is said to him:
﴿Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾, said in the manner of mockery and scorn. "Innaka" (that you), meaning "li-annaka" (because you), "ʿAlī" (ʿAlī).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 50:

﴿Indeed, this﴾, i.e., the punishment, or this matter, is ﴿that about which you used to doubt﴾, i.e., you used to be skeptical.
"In gardens and springs" — a substitute (badal) for "in a secure place."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 53:

﴿They will wear fine silk and thick brocade, facing one another.﴾

"Sundus" (sundus, fine silk) is what is thin of the dibaj (dibaj, silk brocade).

"Istabraq" (istabraq, thick brocade) is what is thick of it. It is an arabicised form (ta'rib) of "istabrah" (istabrah). When a word is arabicised it ceases to be non-Arabic, because the meaning of ta'rib (ta'rib, arabicisation) is that it is made Arabic by altering it, changing it from its original pattern, and subjecting it to the forms of i'rab (i'rab, inflection of the word's endings). Thus it is permissible for it to occur in the Arabic Qur'an.

﴿Facing one another﴾: in their assemblies. This is most complete for intimacy (al-uns).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 54:

﴿Thus it is.﴾ The kaf (ك) is in the nominative case (marfu'ah), meaning: the matter is thus.

﴿And We shall wed them﴾, i.e., We shall pair them with, and this is why it is transitive with the particle bi (ba').

﴿to fair ones with large, lustrous eyes (hur)﴾, the plural of "hawra'" (ḥawrā'), which is one whose eye is intensely black in its blackness and intensely white in its whiteness.

﴿with wide, beautiful eyes (ʿin)﴾, the plural of "ʿaynā'" (ʿaynā'), which is one who has wide eyes.

﴿They call for therein﴾: they ask for [it] in Paradise,

﴿with every fruit, secure﴾: from its ending and its cessation, and from harm arising from excess of it.

(p-296) ﴿They will not taste therein﴾, i.e., in the Garden,

﴿death﴾, ever,

﴿except the first death﴾: except other than the first death, which they tasted in the world. And it has been said: rather, the death they have already tasted was in the world.

﴿And He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 44, verse 57:

﴿As a bounty from your Lord⦆ meaning: for the sake of bounty. It is then a object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), or an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for what precedes it, because His saying, "and He protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire," is a favour from Him to them, since the servant does not deserve anything from God.

﴿That﴾ meaning: the averting of punishment and the entry into Paradise,

﴿that is the supreme triumph.﴾

Note on the translation: the Qur'anic quotations are rendered as they stand in the source, with the ﴿ ﴾ markers retained.

So We have made it easy, [the Book], in your tongue, that they may remember.

[Commentary:] "So We have made it easy" (فَإنَّما يَسَّرْناهُ), i.e., the Book (اَلْكِتابَ), whose mention has already occurred at the beginning of the surah.

"In your tongue, that they may remember" (بِلِسانِكَ لَعَلَّهم يَتَذَكَّرُونَ), i.e., they may take heed (يَتَّعِظُونَ).

﴿So wait﴾, meaning wait for what will befall them.

﴿Indeed they are waiting﴾, meaning they are waiting for the misfortunes that will befall you.
